title: What Is a Supply Chain Network? How Retailers and Suppliers Connect
summary: What is a supply chain network? Learn the two meanings and how retailers and suppliers connect through shared documents and rules.
body_markdown:
In this article, learn about:


-


The two meanings of supply chain network, and which one matters when a supplier adds a retailer


-


The documents that move between a retailer and a supplier


-


Why each new retailer can become its own project, and how a shared network changes that


---


A supply chain network is an interconnected system of suppliers, manufacturers, distributors, retailers, and logistics providers that move products from production to the end customer. It includes the physical facilities and transportation routes that move goods, as well as the technology and information exchanged between trading partners.


For suppliers selling through retail channels, a large part of this network is how they connect with retailers to exchange purchase orders, shipping information, invoices, and other business documents.


Each retailer brings its own requirements, making those connections increasingly complex as a supplier grows. A shared trading partner network can simplify that process by helping businesses establish and maintain connections across multiple retail partners.


This guide explains how supply chain networks work, the role of[electronic data interchange](https://www.spscommerce.com/what-is-edi/) (EDI), and what suppliers should consider when connecting with new retailers.


## Why Does Supply Chain Network Mean Two Things?


Search results for the phrase mix two different ideas, and each one refers to a different job.


A **designed network** is a plan for how one company structures its supply chain, including where facilities sit, which lanes connect them, and how goods flow. A[Fraunhofer review](https://publica.fraunhofer.de/handle/publica/381398) describes supply chain design as the strategic, long-range work of deciding how a supply chain is laid out and run.


That is a separate job from connecting a retailer and a supplier. Readers who need network design should start with a planning or modeling resource instead.


A **joined network** is the shared set of documents, requirements, and relationships that connect a retailer and a supplier, such as the order and shipping formats a retailer requires. It either already exists when a supplier arrives or gets built from scratch for each new retailer.


This table compares the two:


**Question**


**Network You Design**


**Network You Join**


**Who decides?**


One company's planners


The retailer and supplier, guided by the retailer's requirements


**What does it cover?**


Facilities, lanes, and flows


Documents, requirements, and relationships between companies


**What do you walk away with?**


A plan for how to structure the chain


A working connection for orders, shipping, and invoices


## What Moves Through a Trading Partner Network?


A trading partner network moves one order cycle and each step has its own electronic document. Retailers and suppliers usually send these through EDI, which is a shared format that both systems read.


The core cycle has four documents, shown here with their standard[EDI document codes](https://www.spscommerce.com/resources/edi-documents-transactions/) :


-


**Purchase order (PO),**[EDI 850](https://www.spscommerce.com/edi-document/edi-850-purchase-order/) : the retailer's order for items, quantities, and delivery details


-


**Purchase order acknowledgment,**[EDI 855](https://www.spscommerce.com/edi-document/edi-855-purchase-order-acknowledgment/) : the supplier's reply confirming it can fill the order


-


**Advance ship notice (ASN),**[EDI 856](https://www.spscommerce.com/edi-document/edi-856-advance-shipping-notice/) : what is in a shipment, sent so the retailer can plan receiving


-


**Invoice,**[EDI 810](https://www.spscommerce.com/edi-document/edi-810-electronic-invoice/) : the supplier's bill after the goods ship


Item and inventory data move alongside them. Inventory advice ([EDI 846](https://www.spscommerce.com/edi-document/edi-846-inventory-feed/) ) shares stock levels, and product activity data ([EDI 852](https://www.spscommerce.com/edi-document/edi-852-product-activity/) ) reports sales and inventory.


Connections often break when the retailer’s and supplier’s versions of a document differ. For example, a supplier may send an ASN after the truck reaches the dock, so the retailer's receiving team may log the delivery as non-compliant.


**Related Reading:**[EDI Structure Explained: Segments, Elements, and Transaction Sets](https://www.spscommerce.com/community/articles/what-is-edi)


## Why Does Every New Retailer Feel Like a New Project?


Every retailer has its own formats, timelines, and packing rules. A missed rule can turn a shipment into a chargeback, which is a deduction taken from the supplier's payment.


Under a one-off model, a supplier repeats the same work every time they receive a retailer deduction:


-


Gathering the retailer's specifications for each document


-


Mapping the supplier's data to the retailer's format


-


Testing the connection until the retailer approves it


-


Reworking the map each time the retailer updates a requirement


The open question then, is who absorbs a retailer's rule change? In a one-off model, the supplier's team does. In a shared model, the[network applies the change once](https://www.spscommerce.com/why-sps/intelligent-supply-chain-network/) for every affected supplier, so no one is rebuilding the same map.


**Related Reading:**[EDI Chargebacks Explained](https://www.spscommerce.com/community/articles/edi-chargebacks-explained)


## What Do Supply Chain Network Examples Look Like?


Three SPS Commerce customers show how a shared connection works for retailers and suppliers.


### Retail Supply Chain Network Cases


Sporting goods retailer Scheels moved from a paper-based system to EDI and kept adding vendors. The[Scheels case study](https://www.spscommerce.com/resources/scheels/) reports 95% of POs arriving by EDI, and receiving time dropping from three weeks to under 48 hours.


Thrive Market, an online retailer, required the purchase order, acknowledgment, ASN, and invoice from its vendors from day one.


According to the[Thrive Market case study](https://www.spscommerce.com/resources/thrive-market/) , more than 400 vendors and distributors now exchange these documents, and the team can see which vendors have not sent acknowledgments or ship notices.


### Supplier Case: Callaway


Callaway Golf wanted to stop building and maintaining its own EDI maps for each retailer. The[Callaway case study](https://www.spscommerce.com/resources/sps-commerce-case-study-callaway/) reports that it connected to trading partners in days instead of months, because existing mappings were already in place.


SPS also manages day-to-day communication with Callaway's trading partners when requirements change.


## How Can You Test a Supply Chain Network Pitch?


Any vendor can call its product a network, so suppliers should put three questions to each pitch.


-


**Whose requirements are already mapped?** The answer should name the retailers on your list, since a general claim about network size does not cover them.


-


**Who handles a rule change?** The supplier's team, the vendor, or the retailer each carry a different workload when a requirement updates.


-


**What does the next retailer cost?** A shared network should make the next connection cheaper in time and effort than the first.


Suppliers still need accurate item data, such as UPC codes and case sizes, in place before the first order, so the network can apply a retailer's rules to clean information.


## Frequently Asked Questions


### What is a supply chain network in simple terms?


A supply chain network is the group of companies and connections that moves a product from maker to shelf. The phrase can describe a network a company designs or one it joins through shared documents and rules.


### Is a trading partner network the same as network design?


They are different jobs. Network design plans where facilities and lanes go, while a trading partner network connects companies that already trade so orders, ship notices, and invoices move between them in agreed formats.


### What does EDI have to do with a supply chain network?


EDI is one common way that retailers and suppliers exchange orders, shipping notices, and invoices electronically. Suppliers that use it are taking part in a joined network, because the retailer's documents and rules define the connection.


### Why do retailers have different requirements?


Each retailer sets its own formats, timelines, and packing rules, so a connection built for one usually needs changes before it works for the next.


## Want To See How a Shared Network Handles the Next Retailer?


As order complexity and retailer requirements grow, suppliers need stronger operational infrastructure to keep up. That creates a natural bridge from the network concept to the[Intelligent Supply Chain Network](https://www.spscommerce.com/why-sps/intelligent-supply-chain-network/) from SPS, which is one way for a supplier to join a shared network.
